title: Generics
intro: A generic function or type is written once with a placeholder, `T`, and the compiler fills it in for each type you use. A bound such as `T: PartialOrd` says what `T` must be able to do, and the body may use only that.

coming_from.go: `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>` is `func largest[T cmp.Ordered]`, with the type parameter in angle brackets. The bound is a trait, so any type that implements `PartialOrd`, including your own structs, qualifies, not just the built-in ordered types.
coming_from.kotlin: `<T: PartialOrd>` reads like `<T : Comparable<T>>`. Rust compiles a separate copy of the function for each type you use, so there is no type erasure and no `reified` keyword: `TypeId::of::<T>()` identifies a `'static` type, and trait functions such as `T::default()` cover the rest.
coming_from.python: `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>` is the 3.12 syntax `def largest[T: Comparable]`, but the compiler enforces the bound. You can't use `>` on `T` unless the bound says it can. Python does not check hints when the program runs; a type checker such as mypy can, but only if you run one.
coming_from.typescript: `<T: PartialOrd>` is like `<T extends ...>`, but the bound is a trait (something the type can do), not a list of allowed types. Any type with `PartialOrd`, including your own struct with `#[derive(PartialOrd)]`, can be passed in.
coming_from.java: `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>` is `<T extends Comparable<T>>`, and you can use `<` and `>` directly. Rust generics are not erased: the compiler makes a separate copy for each type used, so `T` works with plain numbers without boxing.
coming_from.csharp: `<T: PartialOrd>` is `where T : IComparable<T>`, and you can use `<` and `>` instead of `CompareTo`. Like C#, Rust does not erase `T`, but it gets there differently: the compiler makes a separate copy of the function for each type, so no `T` exists at run time (C# keeps it, and `typeof(T)` works).
coming_from.c: C has no generics, so you'd write `largest_int` and `largest_str` by hand or paste text with a macro. Rust writes those copies for you and type-checks them.
coming_from.cpp: Generics are templates with a concept, `T: PartialOrd` playing the role of `std::totally_ordered T`, and each type gets its own compiled copy. The difference is that Rust checks the function body against the bound once, so a missing bound is reported at the definition. A concept checks the call, not the body: a `+` it never promised still fails per type, inside the body.

notes: `T: PartialOrd` means "any type `T` whose values can be compared with `<` and `>`". Without it, the compiler won't let you compare two `T` values.
This returns `&T`, a reference to the biggest item inside `items`, so nothing is copied.
Several bounds: `T: PartialOrd + Display`. Long lists go in a `where` clause after the signature.
Rust makes you state the constraint up front. `largest<T>` with no bound is a compile error, because the compiler checks a generic function on its own, before anyone calls it.

gotcha.title: Adding two `T`s and returning a `T`
gotcha.looks_fine: Adding two numbers of one type gives that type, so a generic `add(a, b)` that returns `T` only seems to need a way to say that `T` can be added.
gotcha.rust_sees: `T: Add` says only that two `T` values can be added. The type of the sum is a separate type, `<T as Add>::Output`, and nothing says it is `T`. So the compiler refuses to return it as a `T`.
gotcha.why: In Rust, `+` calls the `add` method of the `Add` trait, and each implementation chooses its own result type. For `i32` it is `i32`, but for `&i32` it is also `i32`, not `&i32`. `Add<Output = T>` promises that the sum is a `T`, and the compiler's `help:` writes it for you. The toolkit below prints the types.

go.says: Go prints 5 and 3.75. The constraint `int | float64` lists the allowed types, and `+` on a `T` gives a `T` back, so nothing more needs to be said.

kotlin.says: Kotlin refuses too. `Number` has no `plus`, so `a + b` on a `T : Number` finds nothing to call.

python.says: Python prints 5 and 3.75. The interpreter does not check the `[T]` hint when the program runs, so `a + b` is tried with whatever arrives. A type checker such as mypy would reject `a + b` on an unbounded `T`; this site does not run one.
python.code:
def add[T](a: T, b: T) -> T:
    return a + b


print(add(2, 3))
print(add(1.5, 2.25))

csharp.says: C# prints 5 and 3.75. The `INumber<T>` constraint (C# 11) says `T` has `+` and that adding two `T` gives a `T`, so the promise is in the constraint.

c.says: C prints 5 and 3.75. The macro pastes `((2) + (3))` and `((1.5) + (2.25))` before the compiler looks at types, so there is no generic function to check.

cpp.says: C++ prints 5 and 3.75. With no constraint, the template body is checked when it is used with `int` and with `double`. A C++20 concept would check the call, not the body. Rust checks the body once, against the bound.
